title-group.article-title: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.) as a functional feed additive in poultry nutrition: Implications for sustainable poultry production

abstract.p: Modern poultry production faces serious threats from oxidative stress and gut inflammation, which undermine bird health, growth, and product quality. The growing demand for natural strategies to tackle these challenges in sustainable poultry production has intensified the search for functional feed supplements derived from plants. Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.), known for its rich content of essential nutrients and bioactive compounds, presents a promising option as a functional feed supplement. This review explores the potential of beetroot in poultry diets by synthesizing evidence from two fronts: Firstly, well-established mechanistic studies, which demonstrate its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, gut-protective, and various health-protective effects, and secondly, promising research on its application in poultry nutrition. Additionally, this review presents a detailed overview of current knowledge regarding beetroot, focusing on its biochemical components, health benefits, and potential applications in poultry nutrition. While mechanistic evidence supports beetroot’s use in poultry nutrition, direct research within the field remains limited. However, available research regarding beetroot supplementation suggests beneficial effects on feed efficiency, growth performance, egg quality, lipid metabolism, and immune status at moderate inclusion levels (0.2–2 % of basal diet; 2–30g/kg basal diet; 1–30mL/L drinking water), offering valuable insights and highlighting crucial potential fields for future investigation. Finally, the current review highlights that beetroot holds considerable promise as a multifunctional, sustainable, and consumer-acceptable additive for next-generation poultry feed formulations.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
In recent years, natural feed supplements for livestock and poultry have garnered considerable attention as a potential solution to the rising demand for sustainable and safer animal products among consumers. Among various natural alternatives, Beetroot has a high potential to be a feed supplement due to its abundant nutritional profile and numerous biological activities. This traditional vegetable, also known as a dark red root, is an herbaceous, biennial plant of the Chenopodiaceae family, under the order Caryophyllales (Fig. 1). It has gained a great deal of scientific attention recently, due to its abundant nutritional values and therapeutic functions (Kumar, 2015; Dhiman et al., 2021). It is characterized by its bright crimson color and is widely cultivated across different geographical regions (Kumar, 2015). These are also popularly known as golden beet, table beet, red beet, garden beet, or supper beet in different parts of the world (Yulia et al., 2020). The purple-red color of the tuber is responsible for the presence of water-soluble, heterocyclic nitrogen-based pigments named betacyanin and betaxanthin. A volatile bicyclic alcohol, geosmin, is responsible for its distinct earthy, mushy type flavor and fragrance (Bangar et al., 2022). It originated in the Mediterranean region, and because of its increasing demand, it has recently expanded extensively in Europe, America, and Asia (Akan et al., 2021). Beetroot is traditionally used for its health and nutritional benefits (Babarykin et al., 2019b; Hamedi & Honarvar, 2019). It has been used for medicinal purposes since ancient Roman times (Ninfali and Angelino, 2013). The majority of beetroot is consumed as a vegetable, but it can also be made into a powder and used as a food coloring additive (Domínguez et al., 2020; Kohajdová et al., 2018). Due to the growing interest in eating healthy food, red beetroot has become popular in a variety of cuisines (Clifford et al., 2015).Fig. 1
Raw Beta vulgaris (beetroot).Fig 1 dummy alt text

Beetroot’s potential as a poultry feed supplement can be a significant focus of attention in the coming days due to its impressive nutritional composition. It is rich in biologically active components, including B-vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, and B12), betalains, carotenoids, phenols, folate, minerals, and fiber (Kale et al., 2018). Additionally, beetroot provides important macro and micronutrients, including potassium, iron, calcium, copper, sodium, and zinc (Brzezińska-Rojek et al., 2023; Nowacka et al., 2019). The presence of these compounds, combined with its low-energy sugars and inorganic nitrate content, makes beetroot an attractive natural supplement for animal nutrition (Ceclu and Nistor, 2020; Clifford et al., 2015). Betacyanins, including phenolic acids, caffeic acids, flavonoids, and ascorbic acid, are responsible for the overall antioxidant and antiradical effects of beetroot.

The growing interest in beetroot as a functional feed ingredient is also aligned with the current trend toward reducing synthetic additives in animal production. As consumers increasingly seek animal products produced with natural supplements, beetroot presents an opportunity to meet this demand while potentially improving animal welfare and performance. The demonstrated effects of beetroot on various physiological functions, including its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and nutritional properties (Clifford et al., 2015; Guldiken et al., 2016), suggest multiple potential benefits for poultry production systems (Fig. 2).Fig. 2
Beneficial effects of beetroot’s bioactive compounds on health. (Created with Biorender.com).Fig 2 dummy alt text

Research on the application of beetroot in poultry nutrition represents a promising but still developing area. Available studies indicate improvements in growth rate, feed efficiency, lipid metabolism, hematological indices, and egg quality at moderate inclusion levels. However, poultry-specific evidence remains limited, and the mechanistic basis and optimal usage parameters are yet to be clearly defined. Therefore, this review synthesizes current mechanistic evidence on B. vulgaris bioactives and critically examines their prospective roles in poultry nutrition. Emphasis is placed on antioxidative, anti-inflammatory, and gastrointestinal protective mechanisms, translational relevance to poultry physiology, and future research priorities for sustainable poultry production systems.

sec.title: Botanical classification of beetroot
sec.p:
Beetroot is a biennial herbaceous plant with a short stem and a well-developed, fleshy taproot up to 120 cm in height (Ceclu and Nistor, 2020). The leaves are alternate, simple, and long-petiolate, forming a basal rosette. Leaf blades are ovate to heart-shaped, soft in texture, and prominently veined, with entire to slightly wavy margins. The taxonomical classification of B. vulgaris is shown in (Table 1). The flowers are small, greenish, and bisexual, arranged in dense axillary and terminal inflorescences (Barnóczki et al., 2010). Floral structures are inconspicuous and mainly adapted for wind pollination. The fruits occur as small, dry, aggregated units, each containing a single seed. Beetroot is widely cultivated in different parts of the world and is known by various local names (Székely and Máté, 2022).Table 1

There are several types of beetroots, such as Bulls Blood, Sunset, Crimson Globe, Chioggia, Egyptian Early Yellow, among others. Most of these varieties are commonly produced for their greens and nourishing tap roots (Mudgal et al., 2022).

sec.title: Chemical composition of beetroot
sec.p:
Researchers have determined the nutritive value, active components, and health benefits of beetroot for humans as well as animals. Several varieties of beetroot have been identified as a source of active substances that can be used to optimize the growth performance of poultry. Typically, the approximate moisture present in raw beetroot is 87.4 to 91.3 g/100gm; crude protein (CP) 1.04 to 1.89 g/100gm; Ash 1.08 to 1.4 g/100gm; crude fat 0.15 to 0.3 g/100gm; crude fiber 1.9 to 3.25 g/100gm; carbohydrates 7.23 to 9.05 g/100gm (Ceclu and Nistor, 2020; Kale et al., 2018; Sakhare et al., 2019). sec.title: Bioactive constituents of beetroot
sec.p: Beetroot is rich in a diverse range of biologically active compounds that support its antioxidant and health-promoting functions. Major phytochemical groups include carotenoids, betalains, polyphenols, flavonoids, and saponins (Figiel, 2010; Kaur and Singh, 2014; Nistor et al., 2017). Among these, betalains comprising red violet betacyanins (e.g., betanin) and yellow betaxanthins (e.g., vulgaxanthin) are the most abundant pigments, with total concentrations ranging from 291 to 380 mg per 100 g of fresh weight (Attia et al., 2013; Sakhare et al., 2019). Total phenolic compounds are reported between 82.01 and 128.056 mg gallic acid equivalents per 100 g dry matter (Kavalcová et al., 2015). The result of the analytical quantitative phytochemical measurement indicates the presence of alkaloids (128.889 mg), steroids (16.4 mg), glycosides (0.652 mg), flavonoids (6.417 mg), terpenoids (115.5 mg), saponins (3.789 mg), and acidity level (5.227 mg), that all in per 100g of raw beetroot (Odoh et al., 2012). The relative abundance and structural diversity of these constituents support beetroot’s multifunctional bioactivity, including oxidative stress reduction, immune modulation, and metabolic regulation.

sec.title: Antioxidant properties
sec.p:
Diets high in natural antioxidants are increasingly being used to help animals eliminate excess free radicals from their bodies (Li et al., 2018) and support their regular physiological functions (Lee et al., 2016). Beetroot is the most abundant source of "betalains," which are nitrogen-derived water-soluble pigments that include red-purple betacyanins and yellow betaxanthins (Akan et al., 2021). Along with betalains, beetroot's diverse bioactive compounds act as antioxidants and antiradicals, preventing oxidative stress-related diseases (Fig. 3).Fig. 3
Schematic diagram of the mechanistic pathways underlying the antioxidant effects of beetroot bioactive compounds. (Created with Biorender.com).Fig 3 dummy alt text

Foods high in betalains have been associated with various physiological functions related to health, including those that help scavenge free radicals, inhibit DNA damage, prevent lipid peroxidation, regulate genes, and have antiproliferative, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties (Prieto-Santiago et al., 2020).

Betalains and phenolic acids are capable of donating electrons or hydrogen atoms, thus neutralizing reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) and preventing oxidative damage to lipids and DNA (Martinez et al., 2024). The prominent antioxidant components (betalains and phenolic acids) in different forms of beetroot are presented in (Table 3). In cellular systems, betanin (one kind of betalain) upregulates the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant pathway, leading to higher expression of key enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx) (Martinez-Rodriguez et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). Concurrently, betalains inhibit NF-κB activation, thereby reducing oxidative stress-related inflammation (Martinez et al., 2024). Apart from having betanin, beetroot includes phenolics such as rutin, epicatechin, caffeic acid (Georgiev et al., 2010), polyphenols, vitamin C, and vitamin E, all of which are associated with superior antioxidant properties (Chen et al., 2021). These chemicals reduce oxidative stress and homocysteine levels, thereby regulating vascular homeostasis, tone, and thrombotic activity, including the maintenance of platelet function (Vaitkevičienė et al., 2022).Table 3

Several controlled studies in different animals provide evidence of beetroot’s antioxidant efficacy. For instance, in albino rabbits, oral administration of beetroot juice (0.25g/kg) significantly reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and enhanced catalase (CAT) activity, indicating improved antioxidant defense (Abbas and Ali, 2021). Similarly, studies in rodents have highlighted the capacity of beetroot-derived products to modulate redox homeostasis. In ICR mice, oral supplementation with betalains (0.005–0.08g/kg/day) resulted in a dose-dependent reduction in lipid peroxidation, accompanied by elevated activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), CAT, and glutathione (GSH) (Lu et al., 2009). Comparable antioxidant effects were observed in Wistar rats receiving beetroot juice or extracts, as evidenced by decreased MDA or thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) and increased enzymatic antioxidants, including SOD, glutathione peroxidase (GPX), glutathione reductase (GR), and catalase (CAT) (Kujawska et al., 2009; Michael et al., 2024; Vulić et al., 2014). In another study, betanin's antioxidant capacity was observed to drastically reduce intracellular ROS levels after phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) activation, while also increasing caspase-3 activity in activated neutrophils, underscoring its redox-modulatory and pro-apoptotic properties (Zielińska‐Przyjemska et al., 2012). Studies have shown that beetroot is efficient at protecting cellular components from oxidative damage. In a recent study, beetroot supplementation showed the protection of sperm cells from oxidative damage by increasing antioxidant enzymes in heat-stressed rabbits (Imbabi et al., 2025), indicating that beetroot increases natural antioxidant defenses.

Although the antioxidant mechanisms of beetroot are well established in non-avian models, poultry-specific evidence is currently limited. In poultry, available studies have primarily focused on phenotypic performance and hematological indices (Bakari et al., 2019; Grace et al., 2020; Murad and Beski, 2025), while antioxidant status, oxidative stress markers, and underlying molecular mechanisms were not evaluated.

sec.title: Anti-inflammatory properties
sec.p:
Natural compounds have been employed extensively in recent years due to their advantageous qualities, and studies on them have drawn interest from all around the world. In inflammatory diseases, pro-inflammatory cytokines and other inflammatory mediators significantly contribute to the development of cell damage and tissue dysfunction. Beetroot is widely recognized for its ability to reduce inflammation (Fig. 4). Beetroot's antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties have been assessed in both in vitro and in vivo studies (Tan and Hamid, 2021). Beetroot extracts and betalains have been shown to be effective anti-inflammatory agents. In comparison, betanin (betacyanin, the salient red pigment in red beetroot) exhibits greater anti-inflammatory effects than nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (Hadipour et al., 2020). Betalains and their derivatives have been shown to have protective effects on multiple organs in the body, commencing with the decrease of pro-inflammatory cytokines that increase inflammatory responses, such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-18, and TNF-α (Nirmal et al., 2024).Fig. 4
Schematic diagram of the mechanistic pathways underlying the anti-inflammatory effects of beetroot’s bioactive components. (Created with Biorender.com).Fig 4 dummy alt text

Prostaglandins (PGE2) have a pivotal role in the inflammatory response. Their production is significantly increased in inflammatory tissue, enabling them to induce the cardinal signs of pain, swelling, heat, and redness. The activity of prostaglandin G/H synthases, sometimes referred to as cyclooxygenases (COXs), which are bifunctional enzymes with both cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activity, is necessary for prostaglandin synthesis (Moreno-Ley et al., 2021; Ricciotti and FitzGerald, 2011; Smith et al., 2000). Regarding molecular mechanisms, the betalains are able to decrease the protein levels of the proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-1β), the reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitrogen species, and also the activity of cyclooxygenase-1(COX-1), 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), NADPH oxidase-1 (Nox-1) enzymes, leading to the reduction of PGE2 and leukotrienes level (Ninfali et al., 2017; Nirmal et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). According to reports, betanin specifically inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 in vitro and interacts with the serine and tyrosine residues of the COX active site (Hadipour et al., 2020). Moreover, the NF-κB is a crucial transcription factor that plays a significant role in the pro-inflammatory cascade, because it immediately activates and transcribes the majority of gene targets that control and intensify the inflammatory response (cytokines, chemokines, apoptotic and phagocytic cells, etc) (Baker et al., 2011; Clifford et al., 2015). According to Baker et al. (2011), betalains' anti-inflammatory characteristics involve interfering with NF-κB, which in turn reduces the production of inflammatory mediators such as cytokines and chemokines, as well as phagocyte cells.

Beetroot has gained considerable attention for its potential anti-inflammatory properties, which have been widely explored in different animals. Oral administration of fresh beetroot extract (0.25–0.5 g/kg/day) in rats markedly reduced inflammatory indices such as IL-6, TNF-α, myeloperoxidase (MPO), and NF-κB, while simultaneously enhancing non-protein sulfhydryl (NP-SH) groups and CAT activity, reflecting attenuation of inflammatory stress (El Gamal et al., 2014). Likewise, red beet juice supplementation (0.15–0.3 g/kg) significantly downregulated pro-apoptotic and inflammatory markers, including caspase-3, Bax, matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), TNF-α, and NF-κB, further supporting the anti-inflammatory effects of beetroot-derived bioactive compounds (Raish et al., 2019).

Cell culture studies further elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects. In human endothelial cells, beetroot methanolic extract suppressed NF-κB activation and reduced expression of TNF-α, toll-like receptor-4 (TLR-4), and IL-1β, while upregulating nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), and glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), indicating coordinated anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective signaling (Al-Harbi et al., 2021b). In human hepatocyte (Huh7) cells, betanin treatment enhanced phase II detoxifying enzymes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase-1 (NQO1), while reducing DNA damage, thereby reinforcing the chemoprotective role of beetroot pigments (Esatbeyoglu et al., 2014). Evidence from human studies corroborates these findings. Supplementation with beetroot extract capsules (70–200 mg/day) significantly lowered circulating inflammatory and oxidative stress markers, including TNF-α, IL-6, regulated upon activation normal T-cell expressed and secreted (RANTES), growth-regulated oncogene-α (GRO-α), and advanced oxidation protein products (AOPP), highlighting the systemic anti-inflammatory and antioxidant potential of beetroot bioactives (Pietrzkowski et al., 2010).

Despite extensive mechanistic evidence from non-avian models, corresponding poultry-specific data remain lacking. Poultry-specific evidence is currently limited to emphasizing performance-related outcomes (Selim et al. 2013; Hina, 2023; Prasetyo et al., 2024), in which inflammatory markers and inflammatory signaling pathways were not assessed.

sec.title: Immunomodulatory properties
sec.p: Beetroot has gained increasing attention for its immunomodulatory potential, largely attributed to its rich content of betalains, polyphenols, nitrates, vitamins, and bioactive polysaccharides (Wang et al., 2022). These compounds exert regulatory effects on both innate and adaptive immune responses by modulating cytokine production, immune cell signaling, and redox-sensitive transcription pathways.

Preclinical research in rats with induced mammary adenocarcinoma showed that beetroot extract supplementation increased CD8⁺ T-cells and decreased immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in the tumor microenvironment. These changes suggest that beetroot extract can enhance antitumor immunity and may help overcome chemoresistance through modulation of the immune response (Susilowati et al., 2022). In cyclophosphamide-induced immunosuppressed rats, fermented beetroot extract significantly restored immune function. Supplementation increased natural killer (NK) cell activity and upregulated key immune cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interferon-γ (IFN-γ). These findings suggest that beetroot can stimulate both innate and adaptive immune responses under conditions of chemically induced immune depression (Hwang et al., 2024). Experimental studies in healthy rats have shown that beetroot extract significantly increases leukocyte count, hemoglobin concentration, erythrocytes, and platelets after short-term administration. The increase in white blood cell populations indicates a stimulatory effect on immune cell production and overall immune competence (Hikmawanti et al., 2021). Beetroot extract has demonstrated strong immunomodulatory activity in irradiated animal models. In γ-ray–exposed mice, oral supplementation with beetroot extract significantly enhanced splenocyte proliferation, increased hematopoietic stem cell differentiation, and restored peripheral blood cell counts. The treatment also elevated interleukin-3 (IL-3) levels and improved survival rates, indicating recovery of immune and hematopoietic functions following radiation-induced immunosuppression (Cho et al., 2017).

While immunomodulatory mechanisms of beetroot have been extensively characterized in mammalian systems, poultry studies have largely reported phenotypic immune responses, with limited direct mechanistic validation (Murad and Beski, 2025; Vasiljeva et al., 2018; Sarmiento-García et al., 2023).

sec.title: Gastrointestinal protective properties
sec.p: Consumption of red beet preparations has a substantial impact on almost every digestive tract organ, including the liver, colon, and pancreas. Red beetroot has a slight laxative effect and is widely recognized as an "internal cleansing" ingredient (Babarykin et al., 2019b). The cellulose in beets facilitates stool passage and peristalsis, which helps alleviate constipation and promotes stability for a healthy digestive system (Chaudhari & Nikam, 2015).The discernible substantial effect of red beetroot is to strengthen the stomach and intestinal system, facilitate digestion, and regulate intestinal activity (Şengül, 2021).

Celiac disease, colitis, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and Crohn's disease are important gastrointestinal illnesses that cause inflammation and damage to the intestinal lining. Research suggests that betalains may protect the stomach and intestine from disease-related inflammation and damage (Nirmal et al., 2024). Having more cellulose and fiber in the beetroot substantially decreased the occurrence of precancerous lesions, like aberrant crypt foci in the colon (Babarykin et al., 2019b; Tunnessen et al., 1969). Bioactive compounds (ie., betalains, polyphenols, nitrate, and fiber) have a possible prebiotic effect by influencing the synthesis of metabolites and gut bacteria, which in turn affects host physiology, metabolism, and immunological responses (Danneskiold-Samsøe et al., 2019; Gomez et al., 2019; van der Merwe, 2021). Betalains and phenolic compounds from beetroot can modulate gut microbiota and SCFA(short-chain fatty acid) production, and have antioxidant/anti-inflammatory activity that supports mucosal health (de Oliveira et al., 2021; Martinez et al., 2024).

Studies have shown that beetroot supplementation has a beneficial effect on gastrointestinal disorders. Supplementation with beetroot juice at the doses of 5 and 10 mL/kg, b.w., had reduced the effect of dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) and loperamide (LOP) induced ulcer and constipation in rats, indicating protective effects on gastrointestinal health and intestinal function (Ayari et al., 2025). According to Adekolurejo et al. (2023), 2 % red beetroot improved gut microbial richness, modulated SCFA and bile acid profiles in pigs, providing evidence that beetroot influences gut microbial metabolism in monogastric production animals. Another study by Dawood (2025), noted reduced rumen pH with enriched microbial count in Awassi lambs, suggesting a modulatory effect on rumen fermentation and microbial ecology.

Although the gastrointestinal protective effects of beetroot are well documented in non-avian models (Ahmed et al., 2026; Şengül, 2021; Al-Waeli et al., 2021), poultry studies remain limited and have not evaluated intestinal morphology, epithelial barrier function, microbiota composition, or related mechanistic indicators.

sec.title: Anti-tumor and chemopreventive properties
sec.p: In addition to significant antioxidant and anti-inflammatory functions, beetroot phytochemicals inhibit proliferation in breast, liver, colon, and bladder cancer cell lines by inducing both intrinsic and extrinsic apoptotic pathways (Babarykin et al., 2019b). According to reports, beetroot may have the potential to function as a chemopreventive agent by reducing the risk of multi-organ tumor development and demonstrating lower toxicity (Chen et al., 2021).

Several in vitro studies have demonstrated the cytotoxic and growth-inhibitory properties of betanin in relation to various cancer cell lines. Beetroot extracts, including betanin and betaine, have been shown to inhibit hepatocellular carcinoma cell proliferation (Lee et al., 2014). Kapadia et al. (2003), stated that feeding mice betanin (Dose: 0.0025 %) before and one week after the development of either skin or liver tumors resulted in a considerable decrease in the incidence and multiplicity of tumors. Zielińska‐Przyjemska et al. (2012), found that extracting betanin from beetroot led to procaspase-3 cleavage and increased ROS levels in CaCo-2 cells, highlighting its role in apoptosis-mediated growth inhibition. Furthermore, fermented beetroot juice combined with 2-Amino-1-methyl-6-phenylimidazo[4,5-b] pyridine (PhIP) was found to eliminate the cytotoxic and genotoxic effects of PhIP in a rat using CaCo-2 cells (Klewicka et al., 2012). In a recent study, chemopreventive properties of beetroot were exhibited in the HT29 cell line with IC50 (39.03 ± 1.4 µg/mL), explicating the prevention of colo-rectal cancer (Dwijayanti et al., 2025).

Although the anticancer properties of beetroot have been extensively reported in mammalian models, such outcomes are of limited direct relevance to poultry production systems and should be interpreted primarily as evidence of broader cellular regulatory potential rather than as production-related benefits.

sec.title: Nutritional properties
sec.p: The health benefits of beetroot have led to it becoming a popular "super food" (Mudgal et al., 2022). Red beets are a vegetable with a moderate calorie value that is high in proteins, soluble fibers, carbohydrates, and starch but low in fat. The vitamins C, A, E, and K are abundant in beet roots. B-vitamins (B1-thiamine, B2-riboflavin, B3-niacin, B5-pantothenic acid, B6-pyridoxine, B9-folates, and B12-cyancobalamin) and potent antioxidants, including triterpenes, sesquiterpenoids, carotenoids, coumarins, flavonoids (tiliroside, astragalin, rhamnocitrin, rhamnetin, and kaempferol), betalains, and phenolic compounds, are also present in significant amounts. Saponins, alkaloids (calystegine B1, calystegine B2, calystegine C1, calystegine B3, ipomine), amino acids (threonine, valine, cystine, methionine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, histidine, arginine, glutamic acid, proline, alanine, and tyrosine in leaves), and tannins are additional bioactive substances present in beets. Minerals such as manganese (excellent for bone health), magnesium, potassium, sodium, phosphorus, iron, zinc, copper, boron, silica, and selenium can be found in beet roots (Babarykin et al., 2019b; Ceclu & Nistor, 2020; Lechner & Stoner, 2019; Neelwarne and Halagur, 2013).

Beets are a rich source of vitamin C, fiber, manganese, and potassium. Potassium promotes nerve and muscle health by lowering ATP consumption in the muscles (Jiang et al., 2024). A significant amount of nutritional substances belong to beetroot, and those that have a tremendous impact, including antioxidant, antidepressant, antimicrobial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, diuretic, expectorant, carminative (Jasmitha et al., 2018) hepatoprotective (Olumese and Oboh, 2018) as well as protective of the health of the cardiovascular system (Babarykin et al., 2019b).

sec.title: Application of beetroot in diverse non-avian models
sec.p:
Beetroot is a source of dietary fiber, antioxidants, and nutrients that are beneficial to the health of animals. Several studies have been done on multiple animal species, including laboratory animals, over the years. sec.title: Translational relevance of beetroot bioactives to poultry physiology
sec.p: Mechanistic evidence supporting the antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, vascular, and gut-protective effects of beetroot is well established in mammalian and in vitro models. In poultry, available studies primarily demonstrate improvements in growth performance, feed efficiency, production performance, oxidative biomarkers, immune indices, and selected gut health parameters, while direct molecular and cellular validation remains limited. While direct molecular investigations in poultry remain limited, the convergence of conserved biological pathways and observed productive responses supports the translational relevance of beetroot bioactives. Collectively, these findings justify further poultry-specific mechanistic research and reinforce beetroot’s potential for sustainable poultry production systems.

sec.title: Beetroot as a feed additive in poultry nutrition
sec.p: Research on the use of beetroot in poultry feeding is steadily increasing, with emerging studies reporting potential benefits for productivity, physiological status, and product quality across poultry species. Beetroot’s rich composition of betalains, polyphenols, nitrates, and minerals provides a biochemical basis for its functional properties. Available poultry studies indicate improvements in antioxidant status, gut health-related indices, and selected performance traits following beetroot supplementation. In contrast, most detailed mechanistic insights into beetroot biomolecules, particularly those related to oxidative stress regulation, inflammatory signaling, vascular function, and intestinal protection, have been derived from non-avian animal models. While direct mechanistic studies in poultry are scarce, the underlying cellular processes are largely conserved among vertebrates. These shared mechanisms support the hypothesis that beetroot, used as a functional feed additive, may contribute to improved physiological resilience, nutrient utilization, and productivity in poultry, particularly under metabolic or environmental stress conditions.

sec.p:

According to Murad & Beski (2025), supplementation of beetroot in broilers at the doses of 0, 2, 4, 6 (g/kg) and 0, 2, 4, 6 (mL/L) reported improvement in body weight gain and FCR, indicating enhanced growth performance and feed efficiency. Likewise, a marked improvement in feed conversion ratio (FCR) was observed at 0.4 % (beetroot powder) inclusion, particularly in quail (Sarmiento-García et al., 2023). Moreover, dietary beetroot inclusion has been shown to improve carcass characteristics. Growing geese fed 15 g/kg of beetroot powder along with 15 ml/liter of aqueous extract in drinking water displayed improved carcass traits, suggesting enhanced growth efficiency and meat yield (Al-Waeli et al., 2021). According to Selim et al. (2013) incorporating 0.5 or 1 % beetroot extract into the diets of unsexed Arbor Acres broiler from 1 to 40 d of age improved the overall body weight gain. Similarly, in supplemented kadaknath chicken, dosing at 15 mL and 25 mL beetroot juice daily resulted in improved bodyweight and FCR, indicating enhanced growth performance (Hina, 2023). In another study on laying hens, dietary supplementation with beetroot powder at 0.5 % and 1 % in ISA-Brown laying hens improved the feed conversion ratio (FCR), indicating enhanced feed efficiency and nutrient utilization in laying hens (Ahmed et al., 2026).

The improvements in growth performance and feed efficiency following beetroot supplementation are supported by its positive effects on gastrointestinal health (Fig. 5). These effects are partly attributed to the nitrate content of beetroot, which enhances blood flow, oxygen delivery, and nutrient transport, thereby facilitating improved growth and muscle development. In addition, beetroot contains several bioactive constituents, including betalains, polyphenols, vitamin C, carotenoids, dietary fiber, and other phytochemicals, which collectively contribute to enhanced intestinal morphology. Specifically, improvements in villus height, villus-to-crypt (V/C) ratio, and villus surface area promote greater nutrient absorption and subsequent weight gain (Murad and Beski, 2025).Fig. 5

Supplementation of red beetroot pulp and peel powder dosing at (0.5 %, 1 %, 1.5 %) of the basal diet in laying hens exhibited enhanced egg weight, egg mass, and hen day egg production, indicating improved laying performance (Prasetyo et al., 2024). Likewise, in ISA-Brown laying hens, beetroot powder inclusion at 0.5 % and 1 % of the diet significantly increased egg weight and egg mass, reflecting improved egg production performance (Ahmed et al., 2026). The enhancement in laying performance may be linked to the antioxidant and antibacterial characteristics of beetroot, which can support healthier gut conditions, promoting more efficient nutrient absorption within the digestive tract, which ultimately contributes to improved egg production (Prasetyo et al., 2024). Additionally, red beetroot powder contains a rich supply of essential minerals, which stimulate enzymatic activities involved in protein digestion and synthesis, thereby improving nutrient digestibility and utilization and resulting in increased egg size (Dewi and Wirapartha, 2020). Furthermore, beetroot supplementation improved egg nutritional quality by enhancing yolk fatty acid composition, particularly increasing omega-3 fatty acid content while simultaneously elevating glutamic acid concentration in egg albumen, indicative of improved egg protein quality (Ahmed et al., 2026). Comparable effects have been reported in quail, where beetroot supplementation at the doses of 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 % improved egg quality by increasing omega-3 fatty acid content and reducing saturated fatty acid levels in the yolk, resulting in a healthier fatty acid profile (Şengül, 2021). The reduction in saturated fatty acid levels may be attributed to the suppression of hepatic de novo lipogenesis (Ameer et al., 2014). Beetroot is rich in bioactive constituents, including betalains, flavonoids, nitrates, and polyphenols, which exhibit potent antioxidant activity and metabolic regulatory effects. These compounds are capable of downregulating key lipogenic transcription factors, such as sterol regulatory element–binding proteins (SREBP1/2) (Al-Harbi et al., 2021a), thereby limiting endogenous fatty acid synthesis. Moreover, beetroot-derived polyphenols and betalains can influence elongase and desaturase enzyme activities, promoting fatty acid desaturation and elongation and facilitating the formation of long-chain omega -3 fatty acids (Gonzalez-Soto and Mutch, 2021). Improvements in egg yolk color and retinol content were also observed in birds supplemented with 0.8 % freeze-dried beetroot and 1 % beetroot powder in hens and quail, respectively (De Souza et al., 2019; Şengül, 2021). Furthermore, dietary inclusion of 1 % and 2 % dried beetroot in laying hens enhanced yolk color lightness (L*), indicating improved yolk pigmentation (Kopřiva et al., 2014). Bioactive compounds such as carotenoids, flavonoids, betanin, quercetin, and polyphenols, which have been reported to enhance pigmentation in egg yolk (Kopřiva et al., 2014; Şengül, 2021).

A study of the incorporation of beetroot juice in broiler chicks’ drinking water (30 ml/L) significantly improved hematological parameters such as PCV, RBC count, and Hb levels. Additionally, it lowered blood glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, highlighting its role in enhancing metabolic health (Grace et al., 2020). Similarly, dietary inclusion of beetroot powder and beetroot juice in broilers resulted in significant reductions in serum cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), reflecting improved lipid metabolism and liver function (Murad and Beski, 2025). In a study on Kadaknath chickens, supplementation with 25 mL of beetroot juice per liter of drinking water significantly reduced blood glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, while simultaneously improving hematological parameters such as packed cell volume (PCV) and hemoglobin (Hb), suggesting improved hematological and physiological status (Hina, 2023). Similar hypolipidemic effects of beetroot supplementation have been documented in laying hens. Dietary inclusion of beetroot powder at 0.5 % and 1 % significantly reduced serum total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations in ISA-Brown hens, supporting its role in modulating lipid metabolism and maintaining physiological homeostasis (Ahmed et al., 2026). Consistently, supplementation with red beetroot pulp and peel powder at inclusion levels ranging from 0.5 % to 1.5 % in ISA-Brown laying hens resulted in a marked reduction in serum total cholesterol levels, further reinforcing the potential of beetroot-derived products as functional feed additives for improving metabolic health in poultry (Prasetyo et al., 2024). The hypocholesterolemic effect of beetroot is attributed to the high concentration of bioactive compounds such as betalains, polyphenols, and dietary fiber, which enhance hepatic lipid metabolism, strengthen antioxidant defenses, and suppress lipid peroxidation. The enhancement of hematological parameters is attributed to dietary nitrate present in beetroot, causing vasodilation and a compensatory decrease in plasma volume, leading to higher hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration (Kenjale et al., 2011; Shannon et al., 2021).

sec.title: Antioxidant and immune prospects
sec.p: Beetroot contains a variety of bioactive compounds, including betalains, phenolics, and flavonoids, which exhibit potent antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties. In poultry, these compounds can scavenge free radicals, enhance endogenous antioxidant enzyme activity, and support immune system function, thereby improving overall health and resilience against oxidative stress and disease challenges (Table 8). Though direct measurements of classical antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GPx) or cytokine gene expression after beetroot supplementation are scarce in poultry, a small number of avian studies provide preliminary, supportive evidence, highlighting its potential role in scavenging free radicals and immunomodulatory impacts.

Supplementation of beetroot powder at 0.8 % to the basal diet resulted in decreased DPPH value in quils, explicating the better antioxidant capacity (Sarmiento-García et al., 2023). Likewise, incorporation of beetroot powder and juice at different dose levels in broilers and lohman brown chicken revealed enhanced total antioxidant capacity, as reflected by elevated activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and catalase (CAT). In addition, beetroot supplementation was associated with enhanced immunomodulatory responses in the supplemented groups, as evidenced by increased immunoglobulin levels and improved immune-related parameters (Murad and Beski, 2025; Vasiljeva et al., 2018). This response is attributed to the bioactive constituents of beetroot, which enhance B-cell activity and promote plasma cell differentiation, possibly through modulation of transcription factors such as NF-κB and STAT6 that regulate immunoglobulin production (Ghosh and Hayden, 2008). In poultry, immune modulation through signaling pathways involving NF-κB has been documented in stress and pathogen challenge studies, where changes in NF-κB activity correlated with immune outcomes, and dietary or immunomodulatory factors have been shown to influence B cell–mediated immunoglobulin production (Surai et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2021)

sec.title: Prospects of beetroot in sustainable poultry production
sec.p: Inflammation and oxidative stress represent major challenges in the poultry industry, as their close interaction disrupts cellular homeostasis, weakens immune responses, and leads to reduced growth performance and product quality.

Enteric inflammatory diseases such as coccidiosis and necrotic enteritis (NE) remain among the most significant challenges to global poultry production, contributing to reduced feed efficiency, impaired growth performance, and high economic losses (Mathis et al., 2024; Shamshirgaran and Golchin, 2024). Similarly, oxidative stress in poultry reduces feed intake and growth rate, while worsening the feed conversion ratio (FCR), ultimately impairing production efficiency (Oke et al., 2024). It also damages gastrointestinal epithelial cells and tight junctions, resulting in compromised intestinal integrity, or “leaky gut,” which facilitates pathogen translocation and induces immunosuppression (Mishra and Jha, 2019). In the layer industry, oxidative stress adversely affects egg production, hatchability, eggshell quality, and embryo viability, leading to reduced flock uniformity and significant economic losses (Oke et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021).

In this regard, beetroot supplementation can offer a promising nutritional approach to mitigate inflammation and oxidative stress in poultry. Its rich profile of bioactive compounds supports antioxidant defenses, enhances immune function, and maintains intestinal integrity. Through these mechanisms, beetroot contributes to improved feed efficiency, growth performance, and flock resilience while reducing the need for synthetic additives, aligning with the goals of sustainable poultry production (Fig. 6). Moreover, to detect the improvement of intestinal integrity, which is the precursor of sustainable poultry production, emerging noninvasive bio-sensing technologies for detecting intestinal barrier dysfunction and pathogen translocation may provide valuable tools for future studies assessing the impact of nutritional interventions (e.g., beetroot supplementation) on gut health in poultry (Zhang et al., 2024).Fig. 6

sec.title: Research gaps and recommendations
sec.p: Despite promising evidence of beetroot’s antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and other health-protective effects in rodents and mammals, studies on its use in poultry remain limited. Most available work has focused mainly on growth and production performance, including serum biochemistry, rather than underlying mechanistic pathways. Information on dose response relationships, optimal inclusion levels, and possible antinutritional effects under commercial rearing conditions is also scarce. In addition, practical constraints such as variability in bioactive composition among beetroot sources, stability of bioactive compounds during processing, cost-effectiveness, and potential nitrate-related safety concerns remain insufficiently addressed in poultry nutrition research. To address these gaps, future research should prioritize: (1) dose–response studies to establish optimal inclusion levels of different beetroot forms (e.g., powder, extract, juice) for poultry; (2) long-term feeding trials under commercial production systems to evaluate performance, health status, and product quality; (3) assessment of potential antinutritional or nitrate-related effects, particularly at higher inclusion rates; (4) evaluation under environmental stress conditions, particularly heat stress, which is highly relevant to modern poultry production in tropical and subtropical regions; and (5) integrated mechanistic studies combining biochemical, histological, and molecular approaches to clarify the effects of beetroot bioactives on oxidative balance, inflammatory response, immune regulation, and intestinal integrity in poultry.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This review synthesizes current mechanistic and applied evidence to demonstrate that beetroot represents a promising functional feed additive in poultry nutrition, with potential benefits for growth performance, health, and product quality. Its rich composition of bioactive compounds, betalains, polyphenols, nitrates, and dietary fibre collectively confers antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hypolipidemic, and gut-protective effects. While most mechanistic evidence originates from mammalian and laboratory models, these conserved biological pathways suggest potential relevance to poultry. By integrating phytochemical composition with physiological and productive responses, this review advances current understanding beyond individual studies and provides a structured framework for evaluating beetroot supplementation in poultry. To facilitate practical application under commercial rearing conditions, future research should focus on dose-response relationships, bioavailability, long-term safety, specific environmental evaluation, and production-scale validation. A systems-level approach integrating biochemical, molecular, and sustainability assessments will be crucial to establishing beetroot as a viable, eco-friendly feed ingredient that supports resilient and sustainable poultry production.
